title: A Vetoed Infrastructure Bill
topic: Concept Application · Checks and balances between Congress and the president

modeledOn.label: 2025 AP U.S. Government and Politics Set 1 Question 1 (Concept Application)

prompt: After months of negotiation, both chambers of Congress passed a bill to fund state highway repairs. The House and Senate were controlled by one party, and the president belonged to the other party. The president rejected the bill, arguing that it spent too much. The House then voted 301 to 128 to pass the bill again, but in the Senate the vote was 61 to 39, and the bill did not become law.

parts.label: A
parts.text: Describe the presidential power used in the scenario.

rubricPoints.criterion: Describes the veto: the president’s constitutional power to reject a bill passed by Congress, returning it unsigned with objections.
commonErrors: calls it an executive order
describes a pocket veto when Congress voted again
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: The president used the veto, refusing to sign the bill and sending it back to Congress.
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: The president issued an executive order.

parts.label: B
parts.text: Explain why the bill did not become law even though a majority in both chambers voted for it again.

rubricPoints.criterion: Explains that overriding a veto requires a two-thirds vote in both chambers; the House reached two-thirds (301 of 429), but the Senate’s 61 votes fell short of the 67 needed.
commonErrors: says a simple majority overrides
says the House fell short
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: An override requires two-thirds of each chamber. The House cleared it, but 61 senators is fewer than the 67 required.
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: The Supreme Court struck it down.

parts.label: C
parts.text: Explain how divided government contributed to the outcome in the scenario.

rubricPoints.criterion: Explains that with Congress and the presidency controlled by different parties, the president had partisan incentives to block the majority’s bill, and the minority party in the Senate held enough seats to sustain the veto.
commonErrors: defines divided government without applying it
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Because the president was from the other party, he opposed the majority’s spending plan, and enough senators from his party voted with him to sustain the veto.
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: Divided government is when parties split control.

sampleResponse: A The president used the veto, the constitutional power to reject a bill and return it to Congress unsigned. B Overriding a veto requires a two-thirds vote in both chambers. The House’s 301 votes met that threshold, but the Senate’s 61 votes were short of the 67 needed, so the veto was sustained. C Under divided government, the president’s party opposed the majority’s bill. The president had a partisan reason to veto it, and the minority party in the Senate had enough votes to prevent an override.

parts.label: A
parts.text: Identify the turnout of voters aged 18–29 in the midterm year.

rubricPoints.criterion: Identifies 24 percent.

parts.label: B
parts.text: Describe a pattern in the data.

rubricPoints.criterion: Describes a pattern such as turnout rising with age in both years, or turnout being lower in the midterm year for every age group.
commonErrors: describes a single value only
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: In both years, turnout increases with each older age group.

parts.label: C
parts.text: Draw a conclusion about how a candidate’s campaign could use the pattern you described in part B.

rubricPoints.criterion: Draws a plausible conclusion, such as a midterm campaign focusing outreach and issues on older voters, or investing in get-out-the-vote drives for younger voters.
commonErrors: restates the data without a conclusion

parts.label: D
parts.text: Explain how a factor that influences political participation could account for the difference in turnout between the youngest and oldest voters.

rubricPoints.criterion: Explains a factor such as older voters having more stable residences (registration is easier), stronger party identification, greater political efficacy, or more experience voting.
commonErrors: names a factor without connecting it to age
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Young voters move often, so they must re-register more frequently, which lowers their turnout compared with older voters who have lived in one place for years.

C A midterm campaign would focus its resources and messages on older voters, who make up a larger share of the people who actually vote in midterms. D Younger voters move more often and must re-register after each move, which raises the cost of voting; older voters with stable residences face fewer barriers, so they turn out at higher rates.

title: Student Speech: Tinker and Morse
topic: SCOTUS Comparison · First Amendment speech in public schools

modeledOn.label: 2025 AP U.S. Government and Politics Set 1 Question 3 (SCOTUS Comparison)

prompt: In 2002, students in Juneau, Alaska, were released from class to watch the Olympic torch relay pass their school. A high school student unfurled a 14-foot banner reading “BONG HiTS 4 JESUS” across the street. The principal confiscated the banner and suspended the student, who sued, arguing that his speech was protected. In Morse v. Frederick (2007), the Supreme Court ruled 5–4 that the school did not violate the student’s rights, because schools may restrict student speech at a school-supervised event that can reasonably be viewed as promoting illegal drug use. Base your response on the description of Morse v. Frederick and your knowledge of Tinker v. Des Moines Independent Community School District (1969).

parts.label: A
parts.text: Identify the constitutional provision that is the basis for both Tinker v. Des Moines and Morse v. Frederick.

rubricPoints.criterion: Identifies the First Amendment’s free speech clause (applied to the states through the Fourteenth Amendment).
commonErrors: identifies the Fourth Amendment
identifies the establishment clause
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: The free speech clause of the First Amendment.

parts.label: B
parts.text: Explain how the facts in Tinker v. Des Moines and Morse v. Frederick led to different holdings.

rubricPoints.criterion: Describes relevant facts or the holding of Tinker: students wore black armbands to protest the Vietnam War, and the Court held this symbolic political speech was protected because it did not substantially disrupt school.
commonErrors: confuses Tinker with a flag-burning case
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: In Tinker, students wore armbands to protest the Vietnam War, and the Court ruled that students do not lose their free speech rights at school.

rubricPoints.criterion: Explains the different outcomes: Tinker involved peaceful political speech that caused no substantial disruption, so it was protected; Morse involved a message reasonably read as promoting illegal drug use at a school event, which the school could restrict.
commonErrors: describes both cases without comparing their facts
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: The armbands were political protest that did not disrupt learning, but the banner promoted drug use at a school-supervised event, so the Court allowed the school to restrict it.
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: One student won and the other lost.

parts.label: C
parts.text: Explain how the holding in Morse v. Frederick reflects the balance between individual liberty and social order.

rubricPoints.criterion: Explains that Morse limited a student’s individual expression to protect the school’s interest in maintaining order and discouraging illegal drug use, showing that civil liberties can be restricted when the government has a strong interest.
commonErrors: describes the case without addressing the balance
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: The Court let the school limit one student’s speech to protect its mission of deterring drug use, favoring order over individual expression in that setting.

sampleResponse: A The free speech clause of the First Amendment. B In Tinker, students wore black armbands to protest the Vietnam War; the Court held that this symbolic political speech was protected because it did not substantially disrupt the school. In Morse, the banner was displayed at a school-supervised event and could reasonably be read as promoting illegal drug use, so the Court held the school could restrict it. Peaceful political speech was protected, while pro-drug speech at a school event was not. C Morse shows the Court balancing liberty against order: it allowed a school to limit a student’s expression to protect its interest in deterring illegal drug use among students.

title: How Strong Should the Presidency Be?
topic: Argument Essay · Presidential power and checks and balances

modeledOn.label: 2025 AP U.S. Government and Politics Set 1 Question 4 (Argument Essay)

prompt: Develop an argument that explains whether the Constitution gives the president too much power or an appropriate amount of power. Use at least one piece of evidence from one of the following foundational documents: the Constitution of the United States (Article II), Federalist No. 51, Federalist No. 70. In your response you should: articulate a defensible claim or thesis that responds to the prompt and establishes a line of reasoning; support your claim with at least two pieces of specific and relevant evidence, one from a listed document and one from a different listed document or your knowledge of course concepts; use reasoning to explain why your evidence supports your claim; and respond to an opposing or alternate perspective using refutation, concession, or rebuttal.

parts.label: Essay
parts.text: Write your argument essay.

rubricPoints.criterion: Responds to the prompt with a defensible claim or thesis about presidential power that establishes a line of reasoning.
commonErrors: restates the prompt
takes no position
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: States a position and previews why, such as the reasons it will develop.
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: Restates the question as a statement.

rubricPoints.criterion: Provides at least one piece of evidence relevant to the topic of the prompt.
commonErrors: gives evidence unrelated to the topic
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Accurately describes one relevant constitutional provision, document, or political example.
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: Refers to the topic in general terms only.

rubricPoints.criterion: Uses one piece of specific and relevant evidence to support the claim, or provides two pieces of relevant evidence.
commonErrors: lists evidence without tying it to the claim
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Uses a specific provision or example and shows how it supports the thesis.
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: Mentions a document without explaining what it says.

rubricPoints.criterion: Uses two pieces of specific and relevant evidence to support the claim, one of which comes from a listed foundational document (Article II, Federalist No. 51, or Federalist No. 70). Requires a defensible claim.
commonErrors: uses no listed document
uses two pieces from course concepts only
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Uses a listed document accurately plus a second specific piece of evidence, each supporting the thesis.
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: Uses two examples, neither from the list.

rubricPoints.criterion: Uses reasoning (classification, process, causation, or comparison) to explain how or why the evidence supports the claim.
commonErrors: states evidence and claim with no connection
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Explains why the evidence leads to the conclusion, for example by showing a cause-and-effect relationship.

rubricPoints.criterion: Describes an opposing or alternate perspective and responds to it with rebuttal, concession, or refutation. Requires a defensible claim.
commonErrors: states the opposite view without responding
rebuts a document instead of a perspective
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Presents the strongest opposing argument and explains why it is less persuasive.

sampleResponse: The Constitution gives the president an appropriate amount of power, because it creates an energetic executive while keeping that executive answerable to the other branches. In Federalist No. 70, Hamilton argues that “energy in the executive” is essential to good government, and that a single president can act with decision and speed in a crisis, which a committee could not. Article II reflects this by making the president commander in chief and giving the power to veto legislation. At the same time, Federalist No. 51 explains that “ambition must be made to counteract ambition”: Congress can override vetoes with two-thirds of each chamber, the Senate must confirm appointments and ratify treaties, and Congress controls spending and can impeach. Because the president has the tools to act quickly but cannot make law or spend money alone, the office is strong enough to lead without becoming dangerous. Some argue that the growth of executive orders and military action without a declaration of war shows the president has too much power. However, executive orders can be overturned by courts and later presidents, and Congress can cut off funding for military operations, so these powers remain checked; the problem is Congress choosing not to use its checks, not the Constitution’s design.

title: An Agency Rule Under Scrutiny
topic: Concept Application · Bureaucratic discretion and congressional oversight

modeledOn.label: 2026 AP U.S. Government and Politics Question 1 (Concept Application)

prompt: A federal agency issued a new rule requiring trucking companies to install electronic devices that limit how many hours drivers can work without rest. Congress had given the agency general authority to “promote highway safety” but had not mentioned the devices. A House committee called the agency’s director to a hearing, and several members proposed reducing the agency’s budget in the next appropriations bill. A national trucking association lobbied committee members to block the rule.

parts.label: A
parts.text: Describe the bureaucratic power the agency used in the scenario.

rubricPoints.criterion: Describes discretionary or rule-making authority: the agency used the broad power delegated by Congress to write specific regulations that carry out the law.
commonErrors: says the agency passed a law
describes an executive order
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: The agency used its rule-making authority, filling in the details of a broad law Congress passed by writing a specific regulation.

parts.label: B
parts.text: Explain how Congress could use one of its powers to influence the agency’s actions in the scenario.

rubricPoints.criterion: Explains a check such as oversight hearings that pressure the agency, the power of the purse (cutting its budget), or passing a law that overturns the rule or narrows the agency’s authority.
commonErrors: names a power without explaining its effect
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Congress could use the power of the purse to cut the agency’s funding, pressuring it to delay or withdraw the rule.

parts.label: C
parts.text: Explain how the trucking association’s actions illustrate an iron triangle.

rubricPoints.criterion: Explains the mutually beneficial relationships among an interest group, a congressional committee, and an agency: the association supports committee members, who in turn shape the agency’s budget and rules in the association’s favor.
commonErrors: defines an iron triangle without applying it
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: The trucking association lobbies and supports committee members, who use their control over the agency’s budget to push it toward rules the industry prefers.
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: An iron triangle has three parts.

sampleResponse: A The agency used its rule-making authority, using discretion under a broad law to write a specific regulation requiring the devices. B Congress could use the power of the purse to reduce the agency’s budget in the next appropriations bill, pressuring the agency to delay or weaken the rule. C The trucking association lobbies the committee that oversees and funds the agency; committee members, who rely on industry support, use hearings and budget threats to push the agency toward rules the industry favors, forming a mutually beneficial iron triangle.

title: Drawing Districts: Baker and Rucho
topic: SCOTUS Comparison · Redistricting and the role of the courts

modeledOn.label: 2026 AP U.S. Government and Politics Question 3 (SCOTUS Comparison)

prompt: Voters in North Carolina and Maryland challenged congressional district maps drawn by their state legislatures. In North Carolina, the majority party drew districts to maximize its seats; in Maryland, the other party did the same to a single district. The voters argued that these partisan gerrymanders violated their constitutional rights. In Rucho v. Common Cause (2019), the Supreme Court ruled 5–4 that claims of partisan gerrymandering present political questions that federal courts cannot decide, because there are no judicially manageable standards for deciding how much partisanship is too much. Base your response on the description of Rucho v. Common Cause and your knowledge of Baker v. Carr (1962).

parts.label: A
parts.text: Identify the constitutional clause that the Court relied on in Baker v. Carr.

rubricPoints.criterion: Identifies the equal protection clause of the Fourteenth Amendment.
commonErrors: identifies the due process clause
identifies the First Amendment
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: The equal protection clause of the Fourteenth Amendment.

parts.label: B
parts.text: Explain how the facts in Baker v. Carr and Rucho v. Common Cause led to different holdings.

rubricPoints.criterion: Describes relevant facts or the holding of Baker: Tennessee had not redrawn its legislative districts in decades, leaving districts of very unequal population, and the Court held that such apportionment claims are justiciable.
commonErrors: says Baker banned gerrymandering
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: In Baker, Tennessee had not redistricted since 1901, so rural and urban districts had very unequal populations; the Court ruled federal courts could hear the case.
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: Baker was about voter ID laws.

rubricPoints.criterion: Explains the different outcomes: unequal population could be measured with a clear standard (one person, one vote), so courts could decide it, while partisan advantage has no manageable standard, so Rucho left it to the political branches.
commonErrors: describes both cases without comparing their facts
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Population inequality in Baker could be measured precisely, but the Court in Rucho found no clear test for how much partisanship is unconstitutional, so it declined to decide.

parts.label: C
parts.text: Explain how the holding in Rucho v. Common Cause reflects the concept of federalism.

rubricPoints.criterion: Explains that by keeping federal courts out of partisan gerrymandering disputes, Rucho leaves redistricting decisions to state legislatures, state courts, state commissions, or Congress, preserving state authority over drawing districts.
commonErrors: defines federalism without applying it
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Rucho left limits on partisan maps to the states, which can create independent commissions or rely on state constitutions and state courts.

sampleResponse: A The equal protection clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. B In Baker v. Carr, Tennessee had not redrawn its districts since 1901, so districts had very unequal populations; the Court held that apportionment challenges are justiciable, opening the door to “one person, one vote.” In Rucho, voters challenged districts drawn for partisan advantage; the Court held there was no judicially manageable standard for measuring too much partisanship, so the claims were political questions. Unequal population could be measured, but partisan fairness could not. C Rucho reflects federalism because it leaves limits on partisan gerrymandering to the states, which can act through state courts, state constitutions, or independent redistricting commissions.

rubricPoints.criterion: Uses one piece of specific and relevant evidence to support the claim, or provides two pieces of relevant evidence.
commonErrors: lists evidence without tying it to the claim
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Uses a specific provision or example and shows how it supports the thesis.
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: Mentions a document without explaining what it says.

rubricPoints.criterion: Uses two pieces of specific and relevant evidence to support the claim, one of which comes from a listed foundational document (Article III, Federalist No. 78, or Brutus No. 1). Requires a defensible claim.
commonErrors: uses no listed document
uses two pieces from course concepts only
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Uses a listed document accurately plus a second specific piece of evidence, each supporting the thesis.
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: Uses two examples, neither from the list.

rubricPoints.criterion: Uses reasoning (classification, process, causation, or comparison) to explain how or why the evidence supports the claim.
commonErrors: states evidence and claim with no connection
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Explains why the evidence leads to the conclusion, for example by showing a cause-and-effect relationship.

rubricPoints.criterion: Describes an opposing or alternate perspective and responds to it with rebuttal, concession, or refutation. Requires a defensible claim.
commonErrors: states the opposite view without responding
rebuts a document instead of a perspective
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Presents the strongest opposing argument and explains why it is less persuasive.

sampleResponse: Federal judges should keep life tenure, because it protects their independence so they can uphold the Constitution against popular majorities. Article III provides that judges “shall hold their Offices during good Behaviour” and that their pay cannot be reduced, which removes the threat of losing a job or salary for an unpopular ruling. In Federalist No. 78, Hamilton calls the judiciary the “least dangerous” branch because it has neither the sword nor the purse, and argues that permanent tenure is the best way to secure judges who will guard individual rights. Brown v. Board of Education shows why this matters: judges who did not face reelection struck down school segregation even though it was popular in many states. Because judges cannot be punished for their decisions, they can protect minority rights that elected officials might ignore. Anti-Federalist critics warned that unelected judges with life tenure would answer to no one and could steadily expand federal power over the states. That concern is real, but judges remain checked: the president and Senate control appointments, Congress can impeach judges and limit the courts’ appellate jurisdiction, and constitutional amendments can overturn rulings, so independence does not mean unlimited power.
